# Continuity

::: {.callout-note}
## Companion reading
This lecture corresponds to C&J §1.2.d.
:::

Intuitively, a function is continuous if a small change in the independent variable produces only a
small change in the dependent variable — the graph has no jumps, gaps, or blow-ups. Before making
this precise, it helps to see why the intuitive idea is not yet a *definition*: it uses the word
"small" twice without saying how small, or how the two smallnesses are related.

::: {#exm-jump-motivation}
\
Let
$$
f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x \ge 0 \\ 0 & x < 0. \end{cases}
$$
At $x_0 = 0$, an arbitrarily small change in $x$ — moving from $x=0$ to some $x<0$ — causes $f$ to
jump from $1$ to $0$, a change of a full unit. No matter how small a step we take to the left of $0$,
the output change stays large. We call this a **jump discontinuity** at $x_0=0$.
:::

**Q: How do we make "small change forces small change" precise?** The idea is to formalize "small"
using neighborhoods.

::: {#def-epsilon-neighborhood}
\
Given $a\in\R$ and $\varepsilon>0$, the **$\varepsilon$-neighborhood** of $a$ is the interval
$$
(a-\varepsilon,\, a+\varepsilon).
$$
Think of $\varepsilon$ as a *tolerance*: saying "$x$ is within tolerance of $a$" means
$x\in(a-\varepsilon,a+\varepsilon)$, i.e. $\abs{x-a}<\varepsilon$. "Small change" becomes "$\varepsilon$
small."
:::

Fix a point $x_0$. We want: the distance between $f(x)$ and $f(x_0)$ stays within tolerance $\varepsilon$,
i.e.
$$
\abs{f(x) - f(x_0)} < \varepsilon,
$$
whenever $x$ is *sufficiently close* to $x_0$ — say, within some tolerance $\delta$ of $x_0$. The key
point is that this has to work for **any** $\varepsilon>0$, no matter how small; but we are allowed to
choose $\delta$ *in response to* $\varepsilon$ — a smaller tolerance on the output may well force a
smaller tolerance on the input.

## The $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ Definition

::: {#def-continuity}
\
Let $f\colon D\to\R$ with $D\subseteq\R$, and let $x_0\in D$. We say $f$ is **continuous at $x_0$** if
for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that
$$
x\in D \text{ and } \abs{x-x_0}<\delta \Imp \abs{f(x)-f(x_0)}<\varepsilon.
$$
:::

::: {#exm-jump-not-continuous}
\
Take $f$ as in @exm-jump-motivation and $x_0=0$. Pick $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$. No matter how small we
choose $\delta>0$, there is always some $x<0$ with $\abs{x-x_0}<\delta$ (i.e. $x$ is $\delta$-close to
$x_0=0$), and for any such $x$,
$$
\abs{f(x)-f(x_0)} = \abs{0-1} = 1 > \tfrac12.
$$
So no $\delta$ works for this $\varepsilon$, and $f$ is **not** continuous at $x_0=0$.
:::

::: {#rem-continuity-at-a-point}
Continuity is a property of $f$ **at a point**. The function $f$ above is continuous at every
$x_0\neq 0$ (@exr-jump-continuous-elsewhere) and discontinuous only at $x_0=0$ — a function can be
continuous at some points of its domain and discontinuous at others.
:::

::: {#exr-jump-continuous-elsewhere}
Show that $f$ from @exm-jump-motivation is continuous at every $x_0\neq 0$.
:::

### The $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ game

::: {#rem-epsilon-delta-game}
It helps to think of the definition as a game between an opponent and you. The opponent challenges you
with some $\varepsilon>0$; you must exhibit a matching $\delta>0$ so that
$$
\abs{x-x_0}<\delta \Imp \abs{f(x)-f(x_0)}<\varepsilon.
$$
$f$ is continuous at $x_0$ exactly when you can win this game **no matter which $\varepsilon$ the
opponent picks**.
:::

::: {#exm-linear-continuous}
\
$g(x) = 3x+2$ is continuous at every $x_0\in\R$.

::: {.proof}
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $x_0\in\R$ be arbitrary. We want $\abs{g(x)-g(x_0)}<\varepsilon$. Compute
$$
\abs{g(x)-g(x_0)} = \abs{(3x+2)-(3x_0+2)} = \abs{3x-3x_0} = 3\abs{x-x_0}.
$$
So if we let $\delta = \varepsilon/3$, then
$$
\abs{x-x_0}<\delta \Imp \abs{g(x)-g(x_0)} = 3\abs{x-x_0} < 3\delta = \varepsilon.
$$
:::
:::

::: {#exr-half-x-continuous}
Show, directly from @def-continuity, that $h(x) = \tfrac12 x - 1$ is continuous at every $x_0\in\R$.
(What choice of $\delta$ in terms of $\varepsilon$ makes the argument work?)
:::

<!-- ::: {.solution}
$\abs{h(x)-h(x_0)} = \tfrac12\abs{x-x_0}$, so $\delta = 2\varepsilon$ works: if $\abs{x-x_0}<\delta$
then $\abs{h(x)-h(x_0)} = \tfrac12\abs{x-x_0} < \tfrac12\delta = \varepsilon$.
::: -->

A Jupyter demonstration accompanying this lecture lets you play the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ game
interactively: pick $x_0$ and a $\delta$, and watch the resulting range of $f$-values shrink (or fail
to shrink) as $\delta\to 0$.

## Types of Discontinuities

If $f$ fails to be continuous at $x_0$, the failure typically has one of three flavors.

::: {#rem-jump-discontinuity}
**Jump discontinuities.** The values of $f$ approach one number from the left of $x_0$ and a different
number from the right, as in @exm-jump-motivation. We will make this precise next week with
*one-sided limits*: a jump discontinuity is exactly a point where the one-sided limits exist but
disagree.
:::

::: {#rem-infinite-discontinuity}
**Unbounded (infinite) discontinuities.** Consider
$$
f(x) = \begin{cases} 1/x^2 & x\neq 0 \\ 0 & x = 0. \end{cases}
$$
As $x\to 0$, $f(x)\to\infty$, so $\abs{f(x)-f(0)}$ is **unbounded** on every neighborhood of $0$ — no
$\varepsilon$-tolerance, however large, can be met near $x_0=0$ by any $\delta$.
:::

::: {#rem-oscillation-discontinuity}
**Oscillation discontinuities.** Consider
$$
g(x) = \begin{cases} \sin(1/x) & x\neq 0 \\ 0 & x=0. \end{cases}
$$
Near $x_0=0$, $g$ oscillates wildly: arbitrarily close to $0$ we can always find points where $g$
equals $1$ and points where $g$ equals $-1$. Indeed, for any $n\in\N$, taking
$$
x_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/2} \qquad\text{gives}\qquad \sin(1/x_1) = 1,
$$
and similarly $x_{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi n + 3\pi/2}$ gives $\sin(1/x_{-1}) = -1$; both $x_1,x_{-1}\to 0$
as $n\to\infty$. So on every neighborhood of $0$, no matter how small, $g$ takes values $\varepsilon$
apart for $\varepsilon$ close to $2$ — $g$ cannot be made continuous at $0$ by any choice of $g(0)$.
:::

::: {#exm-x-sin-continuous}
\
Contrast this with
$$
x\sin(1/x) \quad (x\neq 0), \qquad \text{value } 0 \text{ at } x=0,
$$
which **is** continuous at $x_0=0$: although $\sin(1/x)$ still oscillates without settling down, it is
squeezed between $-1$ and $1$, so $\abs{x\sin(1/x) - 0} \le \abs{x} \to 0$ as $x\to 0$. Oscillation
alone does not cause a discontinuity — it must fail to be *damped out* as $x\to x_0$.
:::

## Summary

- The intuitive idea "small change in, small change out" is formalized using
  **$\varepsilon$-neighborhoods** (@def-epsilon-neighborhood): a tolerance interval
  $(a-\varepsilon,a+\varepsilon)$ around a point.
- $f$ is **continuous at $x_0$** (@def-continuity) if for every tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ on the
  output, there is a matching tolerance $\delta>0$ on the input, so that $x$ within $\delta$ of $x_0$
  forces $f(x)$ within $\varepsilon$ of $f(x_0)$ — think of it as a game (@rem-epsilon-delta-game)
  you must be able to win against any $\varepsilon$.
- Continuity is a property of $f$ **at a point** (@rem-continuity-at-a-point); a function can be
  continuous at some points and not others.
- Failures of continuity come in three standard flavors: **jump** discontinuities
  (@rem-jump-discontinuity), where one-sided behavior disagrees; **unbounded** discontinuities
  (@rem-infinite-discontinuity), where $f$ blows up; and **oscillation** discontinuities
  (@rem-oscillation-discontinuity), where $f$ never settles down near $x_0$ — unless the oscillation is
  damped, as in $x\sin(1/x)$ (@exm-x-sin-continuous), which remains continuous.
